guide_sections.heading: Outcomes of the reference parser
guide_sections.body:
```text
input                      ok      value   message
"12"                       TRUE    12      NULL
"0"                        TRUE    0       NULL
"bad"                      FALSE   NULL    invalid count
"999999999999999999999"    FALSE   NULL    count exceeds integer range
12 (a number)              FALSE   NULL    invalid count
```

The ok column is what separates the second and third rows; their values alone would be 0 and nothing. The long digit string passes the pattern, but `as.integer()` cannot hold it and returns NA with a coercion warning, so the parser suppresses that one warning and raises its own clearer error. Each row has the same three fields, including NULL ones, because `list(value = NULL)` keeps the element.

The option cleanup in the reference runs in this order:

```text
moment                                   getOption("digits")
before change_then_fail()                7
after options(digits = 3)                3
stop("intentional") triggers on.exit     7
after tryCatch returns NULL              7
```

`options()` returns the previous settings, so `previous` already holds digits = 7 when the error occurs.

exercises.approach: Run both inputs through `safe()` and read `ok` before looking at `value`.
exercises.why: "0" gives ok TRUE with value 0, while "bad" gives ok FALSE with value NULL, so the status field carries the difference the numbers cannot.
exercises.wrong: A fallback that returns 0 on any error. "0" and "bad" both become 0, and the rejected row is counted as a real zero, as the broad wrapper in Example 3 shows.

exercises.approach: Pass "0" through the pattern `^[0-9]+$` and convert it with `as.integer()`.
exercises.why: The pattern requires one or more digits and nothing else, and "0" is a single digit, so it is accepted and converts to 0L.
exercises.wrong: Tightening the pattern to `^[1-9][0-9]*$` to forbid leading zeros. That also rejects "0" itself, which this domain allows.
exercises.verify: `safe("0")$value` returns 0L, which the reference compares with `== 0L`.

exercises.approach: Return `list(ok, value, message)` from both the success and the error branch.
exercises.why: Success fills value and leaves message NULL; failure does the reverse. Matching names let one expression collect status for all three starter inputs.
exercises.wrong: Returning the bare integer on success and the message string on failure. Combining results for "12", "0" and "bad" with `c()` turns every value into text.
exercises.verify: `vapply(lapply(inputs, safe), function(r) r$ok, logical(1))` returns TRUE, TRUE, FALSE.

exercises.approach: Wrap only the parse call, handle the specific message it is documented to raise, and re-raise anything else.
exercises.why: Bad input is an expected outcome here, but a missing function or package is a defect. Example 3 shows that a broad handler cannot tell them apart.
exercises.wrong: Placing `tryCatch(..., error = function(e) 0)` around the whole pipeline. A typo, a missing dependency and the word "bad" all return 0 without a trace.
exercises.verify: In Example 3 `narrow("bad")` returns NA, and the typo result shows a message containing parse_cuont.

exercises.approach: Save the previous options and register `on.exit(options(previous), add = TRUE)` immediately, before the code that can fail.
exercises.why: `options(digits = 3)` returns the old setting, and on.exit runs even when `stop("intentional")` ends the function.
exercises.wrong: Restoring with `options(previous)` as the last line of the function. The error exits first, the line never runs, and the session keeps printing three significant digits.
exercises.verify: After the caught error, `getOption("digits")` returns the same value as `old`.

exercises.approach: Suppress or muffle only a warning whose cause is known and whose information is kept elsewhere.
exercises.why: The reference silences the integer-range coercion warning because the resulting NA is immediately turned into its own error, so nothing is lost. Example 2 records its warning before muffling it.
exercises.wrong: Wrapping the whole batch in `suppressWarnings()`. A new warning from a later parser change disappears with no record.
exercises.verify: In Example 2 `warnings_seen` returns the one recorded notice and `value` is 4.
